correlation_matrix_historical.text:
`egarch_volatility_model` and `correlation_matrix_historical` answer different questions. The first asks how volatile a single return series is over time, and whether bad news raises that volatility more than good news. It takes one 1-D `returns` series and models log-variance, using `omega`, `alpha`, `gamma` and `beta`. A negative `gamma` means negative shocks push volatility up more than positive shocks of the same size.

`correlation_matrix_historical` asks how several assets move together. It takes a `returns_matrix` of T observations on N assets and gives the Pearson correlation between each pair. It describes co-movement across assets and says nothing about how volatility evolves or reacts to shocks.

explain.text: `egarch_volatility_model` (EGARCH Volatility Model) applies an EGARCH(1,1) asymmetric volatility model, following Nelson (1991), to a 1-D return series that it demeans internally. You supply the parameters, or rely on their defaults: `omega` (log-variance intercept), `alpha` (coefficient on shock magnitude), `gamma` (leverage) and `beta` (log-variance persistence, with |`beta`| below 1 for stationarity). Because it models the log of conditional variance, the variance stays positive for any parameter values. When `gamma` is negative, negative shocks raise volatility more than positive shocks of the same size.

issues: The bullet saying you want |beta| < 1 for stationarity is a parameter constraint, not a reason to choose the model.
The answer never says the parameters are user-set rather than estimated, which a practitioner may assume the model does.

when.text:
`egarch_volatility_model` (the EGARCH Volatility Model) fits when you want an asymmetric view of volatility in a return series:

- You expect bad news to move volatility more than good news of the same size. The leverage term `gamma` captures this when it is negative.
- You want variance that stays positive for any parameter values, since the model works on log-variance rather than variance directly.
- You have a single 1-D return series (`returns`) and want a conditional-volatility model with persistence (`beta`), a magnitude effect (`alpha`) and an intercept (`omega`) that you can set yourself.
- You want `beta` below 1 in absolute value so the model stays stationary.
- For a different asymmetric model, `gjr_garch_asymmetric_model` is listed as a GJR-GARCH(1,1) asymmetric volatility model (Glosten-Jagannathan-Runkle).
